_comment: Blog corpus, consolidated into one file. Narrative prose with no reliable structural seams, so the blog chunker uses overlapping sentence-bounded windows. Every post carries published_at and product_version_at_time: a blog post is a snapshot of a moment, and stripping that metadata manufactures a timeless claim the contradiction resolver cannot discount.

posts.title: Scaling Zephyr to a million jobs a day
posts.author: Marcus Oyelaran
posts.body:
We crossed a million jobs a day on our own internal billing pipeline last quarter. Here is what we had to change along the way, and which defaults we ended up overriding.

Start by measuring queue lag, not throughput. Throughput is a vanity metric. The number that predicts whether your users notice a problem is queue_lag, the gap between enqueue and first dispatch. Throughput can look healthy while lag climbs steadily, because a backlog draining at a constant rate still produces a constant job-per-second figure. We alert on lag exceeding 90 seconds and page on five minutes.

Tuning the retry policy. The default retry policy is deliberately conservative: max_retries defaults to 3, with a fixed 2-second delay between attempts. That is a sensible starting point for a low-volume queue, but at a million jobs a day a fixed delay becomes actively harmful. Every transient downstream blip produces a synchronised wall of retries two seconds later, and that wall is frequently what turns a blip into an outage. Our retry configuration for high-volume queues sets max_retries to 8 with retry_delay_seconds of 2. Eight attempts with a fixed delay gave us a 16-second total retry window. We would have preferred to spread the attempts out, and the lack of built-in jitter was the single biggest operational gap we hit at this scale. We ended up implementing our own spacing at the handler level, re-enqueueing with a randomised delay_seconds rather than letting the built-in retry handle it.

Visibility timeouts and long handlers. The default visibility timeout is 60 seconds. Our invoice-rendering handler regularly took 90, which meant every single invoice job was delivered twice: once to the worker actually doing the work, and again 60 seconds later to a second worker that duplicated it. Raising the timeout well above the realistic worst case fixed it, via client.update_queue with visibility_timeout=300. If you take one thing from this post: compare your p99 handler duration against your visibility timeout today. Duplicate execution from this mismatch is the most common production problem we see, and it is invisible until you go looking.

Authentication at scale. Nothing special here, but worth noting for anyone automating provisioning. Every request carries the key in the Authorization header, as Authorization: Zephyr zq_live_8f2a91c4. We rotate keys monthly from a scheduled job. Create the new key, deploy, revoke the old one; both are valid during the overlap so there is no downtime.

Batch everything. The single highest-leverage change we made was batching enqueues. A batch call counts as one request against the rate-limit quota no matter how many jobs it carries, so moving from per-job enqueues to batches of 100 cut our request volume by two orders of magnitude and took us from constantly brushing the quota to using about 4% of it.

What we would do differently. Measure lag from day one. Override the retry defaults before you need to rather than during an incident. And check your visibility timeout against real handler durations; we lost about a week of engineering time to duplicate execution that a single comparison would have caught.

posts.title: Why we replaced fixed retry delays with exponential backoff and jitter
posts.author: Jen Okafor
posts.body:
In v3.0 we replaced Zephyr's fixed 2-second retry delay with exponential backoff and mandatory full jitter. This post is about why, because the reasoning matters more than the configuration.

Fixed delays synchronise failure. Imagine a thousand jobs in flight when a downstream database briefly refuses connections. With a fixed 2-second delay, all thousand jobs fail at roughly the same moment and all thousand retry at roughly the same moment, two seconds later. The database, which may have recovered in the meantime, is hit by a thousand simultaneous requests. If that wave fails too, the same thing happens two seconds after that. The retry mechanism has converted a brief disturbance into a sustained, self-reinforcing load spike. This is the thundering herd, and fixed delays do not merely fail to prevent it; they actively manufacture it, because they align every client's retry schedule to the same clock.

Exponential backoff buys recovery time. Doubling the delay after each failure, so 1s, 2s, 4s, 8s, 16s, gives a struggling dependency progressively more room. The first retry is cheap and fast, which handles the common case of a momentary blip. Later retries back off hard, which is what a genuinely overloaded service needs. The asymmetry is the point. Most transient failures resolve almost immediately, so the first retry should be quick. The ones that do not resolve quickly are usually capacity problems, where hammering makes things strictly worse.

Why jitter is not optional. Exponential backoff alone does not break synchronisation. If a thousand clients all fail at the same instant and all double their delays identically, they stay in lockstep; the waves just get further apart. You have made the herd less frequent, not less thundering. Full jitter fixes this by sampling the actual delay uniformly from zero to the nominal interval rather than waiting exactly the nominal interval. Retries spread smoothly across the window instead of landing together, and the load a recovering service sees flattens out. We considered making jitter configurable and decided against it. Every real-world configuration we could imagine where someone disabled jitter was a configuration that would cause an incident. Removing the option removed a class of outage.

The trade-off we accepted. Backoff makes individual job latency less predictable. A job that would have retried at a known 2 seconds now retries somewhere between zero and 2, then somewhere between zero and 4. If you built alerting that assumed a bounded, predictable retry window, that alerting needs retuning, and the total time to exhaust a retry budget grew from roughly 10 seconds to roughly 30. We think that is the right trade. Predictable latency on a failing job is worth much less than not amplifying the failure, and a job that retries slightly later is vastly preferable to a dependency that never recovers because its clients will not stop asking.

What this means for you. You mostly do not need to tune this. The defaults, base 1 second, factor 2, full jitter, capped by backoff_max_seconds, are right for the large majority of workloads. The two cases worth attention: if your dependency has a published rate limit, make sure you are on a version that honours Retry-After, and if you have very long-running handlers, set backoff_max_seconds so the cap is proportionate to how long the work actually takes.

posts.title: Windows support lands in the Zephyr CLI
posts.author: Priya Raghunathan
posts.body:
The Zephyr CLI works on Windows. As of v3.1 it is a first-class supported platform, tested on every release, with Windows 10, Windows 11 and Windows Server 2022 in CI. If you tried the CLI on Windows before 3.1 and gave up, it is worth another look.

What was broken. Our credential store resolved the path to the credentials file through a symlink check written against POSIX semantics. On Windows that check raised rather than returning a result, and because it ran during client construction it failed before any command could execute. Every invocation died with credential_store_unreadable, regardless of whether a symlink was anywhere near the path. It was not a subtle bug. It made the CLI completely unusable on Windows for the whole 3.0 series, and the workaround, setting ZEPHYR_API_KEY to bypass the credential file entirely, was circulating on the forum well before we shipped a fix.

What changed in 3.1. We replaced the hand-rolled path resolution with pathlib throughout, which handles platform differences properly, and added Windows runners to CI so this class of regression gets caught before release rather than by users. Credentials now live under APPDATA on Windows, following platform convention rather than forcing a POSIX layout. Existing ZEPHYR_API_KEY environment variables keep working and still take precedence, so nobody using the workaround needs to change anything.

Shell integration. Tab completion for PowerShell ships in the same release. Add the completion command to your PowerShell profile to make it permanent. cmd.exe is supported for running commands but has no completion; PowerShell is what we test against and recommend.

A note on version pinning. The fix is in 3.1 and later. If you are pinned to any 3.0.x release the bug is still there, and there is no patch coming to the 3.0 series. It is a development-dependency pin or a transitive constraint that most commonly keeps people stuck, so check what you have actually resolved with pip show zephyr-cli. We found several teams who believed they were on 3.1 and were held at 3.0.9 by a transitive requirement from an unrelated package.

What is next. Windows parity for the self-hosted agent is in progress but not done; the agent still has a POSIX assumption in its supervision logic. Managed workers are unaffected since they run on our infrastructure.

posts.title: Five tips for designing job payloads
posts.author: Dani Brummer
posts.body:
This is a guest post. Dani runs platform engineering at a mid-sized logistics company and has been using Zephyr since 2.x.

Payload design is one of those things nobody thinks about until it bites. Here are five habits that have served us well.

First, know your size ceiling. Zephyr caps job payloads at 1 MB, which in practice is generous enough that most teams never think about it. We have pushed payloads close to 900 KB without trouble on batch-import jobs that carry a full record set inline. That said, just because you can does not mean you should.

Second, prefer references over data. Even well under the limit, putting large data in a payload has costs. Every retry re-sends the whole thing, queue storage grows, and debugging a dead-lettered job means paging through kilobytes of inlined content. Write the data somewhere durable and enqueue a pointer: a bucket, a key, and a row count. We moved to this pattern for anything over about 50 KB and our DLQ became dramatically easier to work with.

Third, version your payload schema. Add a schema_version field from day one. Workers and producers deploy independently, so there is always a window where an old worker sees a new payload. Explicit versioning turns a confusing deserialisation failure into a clear, handleable branch.

Fourth, keep payloads flat where you can. Deeply nested payloads are harder to query in logs, harder to validate, and harder to diff when something goes wrong. We flatten to two levels wherever possible. There is a hard nesting limit too, which we have never come close to, but flat payloads are easier to work with long before you hit any ceiling.

Fifth, never put secrets in a payload. Payloads are stored, logged, visible in the console, and retained in the DLQ for weeks. Pass a reference to a secret, a vault path or a key id, and resolve it inside the handler. This also means rotating a credential does not invalidate every queued job.

Closing thought. Payload design is cheap to get right at the start and expensive to change later, because fixing it means coordinating a producer and consumer migration while jobs are in flight. Spend twenty minutes on it before your first production queue.

posts.title: Operational patterns for the dead-letter queue
posts.author: Ravi Shankaran
posts.body:
A dead-letter queue is a diagnostic instrument, not a waiting room. Teams that treat it as the latter end up with thousands of entries nobody looks at and a 30-day retention window quietly deleting evidence. Here is how we recommend working with it.

Alert on depth and rate, not on contents. A DLQ with four entries from four unrelated causes is healthy noise. A DLQ gaining fifty entries an hour is an incident regardless of absolute depth. We alert on the derivative, not the level, and page only when the rate sustains for more than ten minutes, which filters out single bad deploys that self-correct.

Classify before you replay. Group by last_error before taking any action. A DLQ is almost never one problem; it is usually two or three overlapping ones, and bulk replay treats them identically. Grouping by error class typically shows one dominant cause worth fixing and a long tail worth deleting.

Never replay into a broken dependency. Replay re-enters the queue with a fresh retry budget, so replaying while the downstream cause is still failing simply refills the DLQ and consumes quota doing it. Fix first, verify with a single-job replay, then bulk replay. The documented behaviour here is deliberate: replay is manual precisely so that this ordering is possible, and there is no automatic sweep that might replay on your behalf at the wrong moment.

Triage with payloads, not just ids. The CLI listing shows job id, attempt count and error class, which tells you that something failed but rarely which records. Pull payloads when you need to correlate failures against your own data, and pair that with a limit so you are not streaming megabytes while triaging.

Treat PermanentFailure as a first-class tool. If your handler can tell that a job will never succeed, a bad recipient, a deleted record, a malformed input, raising PermanentFailure sends it straight to the DLQ without burning five retries. This keeps your retry budget for genuinely transient problems and makes the DLQ more informative, because everything in it arrived for a reason you chose.

Export before the window closes. DLQ entries are retained for 30 days and then deleted permanently, with no recovery path. If a job matters, export it; a scheduled weekly export to object storage costs almost nothing and has saved us twice.

posts.title: At-least-once delivery and what idempotency keys actually guarantee
posts.author: Jen Okafor
posts.body:
The most common misunderstanding we see in support is about what an idempotency key does. It is worth being precise, because the gap between what people assume and what the mechanism provides is exactly where duplicate charges and double-sent emails live.

What the key guarantees. An idempotency key deduplicates enqueues. Two enqueue calls with the same key on the same queue produce one job; the second returns the original. That is the whole guarantee. It protects against your own producer running twice, a retried HTTP request from a webhook, a user double-clicking a button, or a cron job firing twice after a restart.

What it does not guarantee. It does not deduplicate deliveries. Zephyr is at-least-once, which means a single job can be handed to a handler more than once. Three mechanisms cause this and none of them are failures of the key: a worker claims a job and dies before acknowledging it, a handler runs longer than its visibility timeout so the job becomes visible again, or a network partition hides a successful acknowledgement from the dispatcher. In all three cases the job is delivered twice and the idempotency key is working exactly as designed.

Why at-least-once rather than exactly-once. Exactly-once delivery across a network boundary is not achievable in the general case; what systems advertise as exactly-once is at-least-once delivery plus deduplication at the consumer. We prefer to be explicit about that rather than imply a guarantee we would then have to qualify. Being honest about it pushes the deduplication to where it can actually be correct, which is inside your handler, next to your database, in the same transaction as your side effect.

The retention window matters. Keys are retained for 24 hours from first use. That bounds the guarantee: it is enough for retry storms, duplicate webhooks and double-submits, and it is not a permanent uniqueness constraint. If you need deduplication over weeks, enforce it in your own storage; if you need it over seconds, the key is ideal.

Writing an idempotent handler. The reliable pattern is a completion marker written in the same transaction as the side effect. Check the marker, do the work, write the marker, commit. Checking a marker written in a separate transaction leaves a window where two deliveries both pass the check. If the side effect is in an external system that offers its own idempotency key, pass yours through to it, which is the cleanest option when it is available.

A diagnostic shortcut. If you see duplicate execution, check attempt_count on the job before anything else. If it is above one, you are looking at redelivery, and the visibility timeout against your real handler duration is the first thing to compare. If it is one, you have two jobs rather than one delivery twice, and the problem is on the producer side where the key belongs.

posts.title: Zephyr v3 is here: what changed and why
posts.author: Marcus Oyelaran
posts.body:
Zephyr v3.0 is generally available today. This is our first release with breaking changes since 1.0, and we did not take them lightly. Here is each one and the reasoning behind it.

The authentication header changed. Keys now travel in X-Zephyr-Key rather than the old Authorization: Zephyr form. The old form conflicted with standard proxy and gateway behaviour; several customers had infrastructure that stripped or rewrote Authorization headers in ways that were painful to debug. A dedicated header avoids the whole category. The old form now returns 401 with unauthorized_header_form, which is deliberately distinct from a revoked-key error so the fix is obvious from the response body.

Retry defaults moved from 3 to 5. Our telemetry showed a meaningful share of transient failures resolving on the fourth and fifth attempts, which the old default of 3 never reached. Newly created queues get 5; existing queues keep whatever value they were created with, so nothing changes under you on upgrade. The flip side is that a fleet spanning both eras behaves inconsistently until you set the value explicitly, and we recommend pinning it per queue during migration rather than relying on either default.

Exponential backoff with mandatory jitter replaced fixed delays. Fixed 2-second delays synchronised retries across all clients and turned brief dependency blips into sustained load spikes. Backoff plus full jitter spreads them out. Jitter is not configurable, which was a deliberate decision rather than an oversight.

The default visibility timeout dropped from 60 seconds to 30. Shorter timeouts mean faster recovery when a worker dies, which is the common case. The trade-off is that handlers reliably taking between 30 and 60 seconds, which were fine under v2, now exceed the default and get redelivered. If you have handlers in that band, raise the timeout before upgrading; this presents as sudden duplicate execution after an otherwise clean upgrade and is the one change most likely to surprise you.

Deprecations. client.queue.push is superseded by client.enqueue, which supports idempotency keys and per-job timeouts that push cannot express. push still works and will keep working through the 3.x series. The --legacy-ack worker flag is deprecated and will be removed in a later 3.x release; the two-phase acknowledgement protocol it enables is no longer needed.

On upgrading. Read the migration guide rather than this post for the actual steps. If you only check one thing, check the auth header; it accounts for the clear majority of upgrade support tickets, and it looks like a credentials problem rather than a header problem, which sends people down the wrong path.

posts.title: When a managed queue beats self-hosting Redis, and when it does not
posts.author: Lena Stavros
posts.body:
We are obviously not neutral here, so take this as a structured argument rather than an impartial review. The honest answer is that self-hosting a queue on Redis is a perfectly good choice for a real range of situations, and knowing which situation you are in matters more than the feature comparison.

Where self-hosting wins. If your job volume is low and bursty, a Redis list and twenty lines of worker code is genuinely hard to beat. There is no vendor, no egress, no quota, and you already run Redis. For a single-service application with a handful of background tasks, introducing a managed dependency buys you very little and costs you a network hop and a bill. Latency-critical work also favours local infrastructure; our dispatch path is fast but it is not as fast as a local Redis pop, and if your handler runs in single-digit milliseconds the transport starts to dominate.

Where it stops being a good trade. The crossover is rarely about throughput. It is about the operational surface you did not plan to own. Retry semantics with jitter, a dead-letter queue with retention and replay, visibility timeouts with lease extension, idempotent enqueue, at-least-once guarantees under partition, per-queue observability: each of these is a modest amount of code and a non-trivial amount of hard-won correctness. Teams usually discover they need all of them, one incident at a time, and end up building a worse version of a queue while trying to ship something else.

The honest cost comparison. Compare total cost of ownership rather than infrastructure spend. Self-hosting looks free because the Redis instance is already paid for, but the engineering time spent on the fifth incident caused by a missing visibility timeout is not free, and it arrives at the worst moment. Conversely, if you have a platform team who already operate queues competently, the managed option is paying for something you have.

A practical heuristic. Self-host while you have fewer than about five distinct job types, no hard durability requirement, and nobody has yet asked what happens to a job that fails ten times. Move to something managed when the answer to that last question starts mattering, because that is the point where you are about to build a DLQ.

What we would not claim. We are not faster for trivial workloads, we are not cheaper at tiny scale, and we add a dependency. If someone tells you a managed queue is strictly better, they are selling rather than advising.
